01 · Before you listen

A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
chain of custody
Documented history of who held evidence and when.
culpability
Responsibility for wrongdoing.
contemplated
Considered or planned but not necessarily done.
reconciled
Checked for agreement with other records.
traceable
Possible to follow through reliable records.
disposal record
A document reporting removal or destruction of an item.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Fiona's reference to a missing authorisation register had raised the possibility of evidence more substantial than the delegated-authority sheet. The latter described who was permitted to approve exceptional payments; the former, if it existed and could be authenticated, might identify decisions actually taken. Emma understood the attraction of that possibility. She also understood how little the archive had yet established.

A further inventory search produced a dated reference from 2012. It described an approvals book associated with the student travel programme and assigned it a carton number. The carton was not among those catalogued in the trust's present main store. No verified disposal record had been located.

Sarah interpreted the absence as grounds for suspicion. Emma disagreed with the inference, not with the need to investigate. A box omitted from one location could have been transferred, renumbered, misfiled or mistakenly entered in the first place. Conversely, the absence of a destruction notice did not prove survival. The central question was one of custody, not culpability.

Emma reconsidered the September 2011 delegated-authority document. Its division between requesting an exception and authorising one was clear. It also directed cases above a threshold to the trust chair, although the threshold itself was illegible on the surviving copy. Malcolm Vale had occupied that office. The procedural power to approve, however, remained distinct from evidence that he had exercised it in any identified transaction.

The redacted selection letter shown by Helen Ward offered no shortcut. Its wording indicated conditional selection of one applicant; it could not establish authorisation, bank transfer or receipt. Moreover, nothing linked that application to the exceptional-payment process. Emma would not manufacture a connection merely because two gaps in the evidence seemed to fit together.

Later that afternoon Fiona discovered a second historical listing. The same carton reference appeared on a form describing records intended for an external storage provider. The company name was partly illegible. Crucially, there was no signature or delivery confirmation on the copy Fiona had inspected.

“So the book went to an outside warehouse,” Sarah said.

“The paperwork suggests that transfer was contemplated,” Emma corrected. “Whether it happened is still open.”

A chain of custody, she explained, required more than successive references. The investigators needed evidence that the item was collected, received and retained under a traceable identifier. Even then, the register itself would have to be examined, its dates checked and its entries reconciled against any available payment documentation. A signature, if found, would not automatically establish that the corresponding money had reached a student.

Emma drafted a narrow enquiry for Fiona: identify the storage provider if possible; look for a signed receipt or tracking reference; check later inventories for the carton number or a renumbered equivalent. No private beneficiary information was needed to establish whether the archive had a recoverable book.

The anonymous caller's earlier insistence on identifying payment approvers now had a testable documentary target. That did not make the caller credible by association. The caller's identity, motives and access to the trust's financial records remained wholly unverified.

As evening drew in, Emma drew three successive boxes in her notebook: Listed for transfer, Received in storage, Register examined. Only the first had documentary support, and even that support rested on preliminary descriptions rather than originals inspected by her.

Her final note read: Before asking what the register proves, establish where the register is.
